Proof of Depot-Edge Flow-Rate Uniqueness — Cipolla_ ​

Source page ID: MT8yvInZHhBAiie2MXnOZo | Open in Tencent Docs

Proof of Depot-Edge Flow-Rate Uniqueness ​

This proof makes a few modifications to the original proof to accommodate the generalized form.

Proof of Flow-Rate Uniqueness for Flow Limiters (Cipolla_)

Definition ​

For a directed graph  G=(V,E) and flow limits  c, define the flow function  fG,c:[0,∞)|W+|×[0,∞)|W−|→[0,∞)|W+|×[0,∞)|W−|.  fG,c(x;y)=(u;v) means that when source-depot outflows (hereafter inputs) are limited to  x and destination-depot inflows (hereafter outputs) are limited to  y, the actual inputs are  u and outputs are  v. Here  x,y,u,v are all vectors.

Notation ​

For a vector  v∈Rn, write  ‖v‖1 for the 1-norm of  v, the sum of the absolute values of its components. In mathematical notation:

‖v‖1=∑i=1n|vi|=|v1|+|v2|+⋯+|vn|

For vectors  x,y∈Rn of the same dimension, define the vector comparison  x≤y to hold if and only if each component of  x is at most the corresponding component of  y: for every  i=1,2,…,n,  xi≤yi. Mathematically:

x≤y⟺xi≤yi,∀i∈{1,2,…,n}

Basic Properties ​

For an idealized system  (G,c), the flow function  fG,c(x;y)=(u;v) defined on it satisfies these basic properties.

  • Constraints: u≤x, v≤y

  • Conservation: ‖u‖1=‖v‖1

Comparison Theorem ​

The comparison theorem is an important intermediate theorem used throughout this proof, stated as follows:

For an idealized system  (G,c) and its flow function  fG,c, suppose

fG,c(x,a1;y)=(u1,b1;v1)fG,c(x,a2;y)=(u2,b2;v2)

If  a1<a2, then

u1≥u2,b1≤b2,v1≤v2

If additionally b1<a1, then (the converse need not hold):

u1=u2,b1=b2,v1=v2

A symmetric comparison theorem holds for the outputs.

The model is also symmetric under reordering of inputs and outputs, so the theorem holds for every input and output. Below, only the case of the last input is proved.

The comparison theorem also has the following corollaries, used together with the basic properties of the flow function:

Corollary One ​

For an idealized system  (G,c) and its flow function  fG,c, if

fG,c(x,a1;y)=(u1,b1;v1)fG,c(x,a2;y)=(u2,b2;v2)

then

|b1−b2|≤|a1−a2|

Proof: The case a1=a2 is immediate. Without loss of generality, assume a1<a2 below.

The constraints give b1≤a1, b2≤a2.

If b1<a1, then b1=b2 and the desired inequality follows immediately.

Otherwise a1=b1, and the comparison theorem gives

a1=b1≤b2≤a2

The desired inequality follows in this case too. This completes the proof.

Corollary Two (1-Norm Bound, or Lipschitz Condition) ​

For an idealized system  (G,c) and its flow function  fG,c, if

fG,c(x1;y1)=(u1;v1)fG,c(x2;y2)=(u2;v2)

then

‖(u1;v1)−(u2;v2)‖1≤2‖(x1;y1)−(x2;y2)‖1

Proof: Consider a change in a single component:

fG,c(x,a1;y)=(u1,b1;v1)fG,c(x,a2;y)=(u2,b2;v2)

The case a1=a2 is immediate. Without loss of generality, assume a1<a2 below.

The comparison theorem gives

b1≤b2,u1≥u2,v1≤v2

Conservation also gives ‖u1‖1+b1=‖v1‖1, ‖u2‖1+b2=‖v2‖1, from which we obtain

‖u1−u2‖1+‖v1−v2‖1=‖u1‖1−‖u2‖1+‖v2‖1−‖v1‖1=b2−b1

By Corollary One, |b1−b2|≤|a1−a2|. Hence

‖(u1,b1;v1)−(u2,b2;v2)‖1≤2|b1−b2|≤2|a1−a2|

For changes in multiple components, separate the component changes and add them, applying the triangle inequality for the 1-norm to complete the proof.

Corollary Three (Continuity) ​

For an idealized system  (G,c), its flow function  fG,c is continuous.

Proof: This follows directly from Corollary Two.

Overall Proof Strategy ​

Any idealized system  (G,c) can be built from basic splitters and convergers through disjoint union and recirculation. Mathematical induction can establish step by step that, for every idealized system  (G,c), its flow function fG,c exists uniquely and satisfies the basic properties and comparison theorem.

Basic Splitter ​

For a splitter of out-degree  3, let the input limit be  x and the output limits  (y1,y2,y3). Without loss of generality, assume  y1≤y2≤y3.

Define the flow function  fG,c by

fG,c(x;y1,y2,y3)={(y1+y2+y3;y1,y2,y3)y1+y2+y3≤x(x;y1,y2,x−y1−y2)y1+2y2≤x≤y1+y2+y3(x;y1,12(x−y1),12(x−y1))3y1≤x≤y1+2y2(x;13x,13x,13x)x≤3y1

A similar discussion applies to a splitter of out-degree  2.

It can be verified that fG,c exists uniquely and satisfies the basic properties and comparison theorem.

Basic Converger ​

For a converger of in-degree  3, let the input limits be  (x1,x2,x3) and the output limit  y. Without loss of generality, assume  x1≤x2≤x3.

Define the flow function  fG,c by

fG,c((x1,x2,x3),y)={(x1,x2,x3;x1+x2+x3)x1+x2+x3≤y(x1,x2,y−x1−x2;y)x1+2x2≤y≤x1+x2+x3(x1,12(y−x1),12(y−x1);y)3x1≤y≤x1+2x2(13y,13y,13y;y)y≤3x1

A similar discussion applies to a converger of in-degree  2.

It can be verified that  fG,c is continuous, satisfies the comparison theorem, and is unique.

Disjoint Union ​

Let two idealized systems (G1,c1) and (G2,c2) have disjoint vertex and edge sets. Their union gives a new idealized system (G,c).

The original two flow functions are

fG1,c1(x1;y1)=(u1;v1)fG2,c2(x2;y2)=(u2;v2)

We can define a new flow function  fG,c:[0,∞)|W1+|+|W2+|×[0,∞)|W1−|+|W2−|→[0,∞)|W1+|+|W2+|×[0,∞)|W1−|+|W2−|.

fG,c(x1,x2;y1,y2)=(u1,u2;v1,v2)

Since fG1,c1,fG2,c2 exist uniquely and satisfy the basic properties and comparison theorem, the same follows immediately for fG,c.

Recirculation ​

Recirculation means connecting one input and one output of the original idealized system  (G,c), assigning capacity limit  C. This produces a new idealized system  (G∗,c∗).

The original system's flow function is

fG,c(x,a;y,b)=(u,c;v,d)

where a,b correspond to the edges to be connected.

Define the parameter functions

s(r)=min(C,2C−r),t(r)=min(C,r),r∈[0,2C]

As r increases, (s(r),t(r)) follows (C,0)→(C,C)→(0,C). For fixed x,y, fG,c(x,s(r);y,t(r)) is a function of r, denoted by

fG,c(x,s(r);y,t(r))=(U(r),B(r);V(r),D(r)).

Define the new flow function by

fG∗,c∗(x;y)=(u;v)

if and only if an r∈[0,2C] exists such that

fG,c(x,s(r);y,t(r))=(u,B(r);v,D(r)),and B(r)=D(r).
Proof of Existence ​

At r=0, B(r)≥0 , D(r)=0.

At r=C, B(r)≥0 , D(r)≥0.

At r=2C, B(r)=0 , D(r)≥0.

Existence follows from the continuity of  fG,c. This completes the proof.

Proof of Uniqueness ​

Suppose r1<r2 both satisfy the definition. The definitions of s(r),t(r) give

s(r1)≥s(r2),t(r1)≤t(r2)

By the comparison theorem,

U(r1)≤U(r2),V(r1)≥V(r2)

Since both points satisfy  B(ri)=D(ri), flow conservation gives

‖U(ri)‖1=‖V(ri)‖1

Subtracting the expressions for  i=1,2 gives

∑j(Uj(r1)−Uj(r2))=∑k(Vk(r1)−Vk(r2))

The left side is ≤0 and the right side ≥0, so both must equal 0. Hence

U(r1)=U(r2),V(r1)=V(r2)

This completes the proof.

Proof that the Comparison Theorem Is Preserved ​

Suppose

fG,c(x,a1,s(r1);y,t(r1))=(u1,b1,B1(r1);v1,D1(r1))fG,c(x,a2,s(r2);y,t(r2))=(u2,b2,B2(r2);v2,D2(r2))

By the comparison theorem, when  a1<a2,  B2(r1)≤B1(r1),D2(r1)≥D2(r1).

Together with  B1(r1)=D1(r1), this gives  B2(r1)−D2(r1)≤0.

Also  B2(0)−D2(0)=B2(0)≥0.

Thus, by continuity, choose  r2∈[0,r1] such that  B2(r2)=D2(r2). That is,  r2≤r1.

Since

a1<a2,r2≤r1

applying the comparison theorem twice gives  u2≤u1,v2≥v1.

Flow conservation gives

∑j(ui)j+bi=∑k(vi)k

Subtracting for  i=1,2 gives

b2−b1=∑k((v2)k−(v1)k)−∑j((u2)j−(u1)j)≥0

Thus  b2≥b1, proving the comparison theorem.

All the above proofs establish the depot-edge flow-rate uniqueness theorem.

Translator's note: The source writes D_2(r_1)\ge D_2(r_1) in the last proof. This apparent subscript error is preserved rather than silently corrected.
